analysis.evidence: Abram takes Sarai, already identified as his wife, along with Lot, their possessions, and the people they had acquired in Haran. The next verb, וַיֵּצְאוּ (‘and they set out’), shows that Abram took them with him on the journey to Canaan.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ introduces a Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with Abram as its subject.

draft.change: Link the existing Abram article to אבה through its father element and add Genesis 12:4 as an example.
draft.definition: Abram, son of Terah, later named Abraham. The name means “exalted father.”
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:4 repeats the name אַבְרָם when giving Abram’s age at departure. The name’s אָב element belongs to Haqor’s אבה article.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּקַּח אַבְרָם, Abram is the subject of “took.” The verse identifies Sarai as his wife and Lot as his brother’s son. Haqor assigns the name to אבה through its אָב (“father”) element.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Abram, the son of Terah later named Abraham

analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

evidence.note: The verse explicitly gives Sarai as the name of Abram’s wife.
God identifies שָׂרַי as Abraham’s wife and gives her the name שָׂרָה.
Kings and their noblewomen appear in parallel. The noun for the women, שָׂרוֹת, is the plural of שָׂרָה.

article.name: שָׂרַי
article.summary: Sarai is the name by which Abram’s wife is introduced. Her later name שָׂרָה has the same form as the Hebrew noun for a princess or noblewoman, supporting a similar meaning for Sarai. The text leaves the force of the earlier name’s ending unexplained.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for שָׂרַי linked to the שׂרר word family.
draft.definition: Sarai, the earlier name of Abram’s wife Sarah.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:29 names Abram’s wife Sarai. Genesis 17:15 gives both names when God tells Abraham to call her Sarah.

analysis.evidence: In אֶת שָׂרַי אִשְׁתּוֹ, the direct-object marker אֶת introduces Sarai, and אִשְׁתּוֹ (“his wife”) identifies her as Abram’s wife.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. The final י is part of the name.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Abram’s wife before she was named Sarah.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 66585:4, 66577:3, 66561:4, 66324:3.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular construct noun with the third-person masculine singular possessive suffix ־וֹ.

evidence.note: Terah fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran, and Haran fathered Lot.

article.name: לוֹט
article.summary: Terah’s genealogy names Lot as Haran’s son and Abram’s nephew. The passage gives no explanation of the name.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for לוֹט with its etymology unassigned.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:27 names Lot as the son whom Haran fathered.

analysis.evidence: וְאֶת marks Lot as one of the people Abram took with him. The following בֶּן אָחִיו, “his brother’s son,” identifies Lot as Abram’s nephew, matching the genealogy in Genesis 11:27.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Haran’s son.

analysis.evidence: בֶּן אָחִיו means “the son of his brother” and identifies Lot as the son of Abram’s brother. The possessive suffix belongs to אָחִיו.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 68121:12, 67845:13, 66581:1, 66568:4, 66568:12, 66562:3.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state with a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כָּל רְכוּשָׁם אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁוּ, “all their property that they had acquired,” כָּל takes the collective noun רְכוּשָׁם as its complement and denotes the full amount of their property.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כָּל רְכוּשָׁם אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁוּ, “all their possessions that they had acquired,” אֲשֶׁר introduces a relative clause whose understood object is רְכוּשָׁם, “their possessions.”
analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew relative particle with no prefix or suffix.
